extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (undergraduate/graduate courses and professionals seeking professionalization/accreditation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards about professionalism, ethics, associations, accreditation, and the educational and organizational criteria that define and measure professional public relations practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Identify the six characteristics of professions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the six characteristics of professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a stated learning objective for the chapter—students should be able to recognize the criteria used to judge whether an occupation (including public relations) has achieved professional status; see the six indicators listed under 'Criteria of a Profession.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Describe the major professional associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the major professional associations serving the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to identify and describe roles and functions of organizations such as PRSA, IABC, IPRA, CIPR, CPRS, PRIA, and the Global Alliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Describe recommended undergraduate program
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the undergraduate program of study in public relations recommended by the Commission on Public Relations Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be familiar with curricular recommendations and core competencies promoted by the Commission and by professional organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Identify motivations behind concern for professional ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the major motivations behind concern for professional ethics in public relations practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand why ethics matter (public trust, organizational credibility) and the forces motivating ethical scrutiny of PR practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: List positives and negatives of socially responsible PR
rubrics_metrics.description: List and briefly discuss the positives of socially responsible public relations, as well as the major negatives attributed to public relations when it is not practiced in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to articulate benefits of responsible practice and common critiques when PR prioritizes only organizational interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Outline and apply PRSA Code of Ethics articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline and apply some of the major articles from the Public Relations Society of America Code of Ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to interpret PRSA ethics provisions and apply them to practical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning outcome: Outline arguments for and against licensing and accreditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the major arguments for and against licensing and accreditation of practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand pros/cons such as public protection and standardization versus barriers to entry and professional autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Professional associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional associations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional associations are indicators of status: they publish, hold conferences/seminars, run awards, offer continuing education, advocate for the field, set codes of ethics and standards, and may run accreditation/certification programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Specialized educational preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized educational preparation to acquire unique knowledge and skills
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hallmark of a profession is formalized education and curricula (e.g., Commission on Public Relations Education recommendations, university programs) that produce practitioners with specialized competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Body of theory-based knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A body of theory-based knowledge, developed through research, that provides us with principles of appropriate and effective public relations practice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional status depends on a research-informed theoretical base that informs practice and standards of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Codes of ethics and standards enforced by peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes of ethics and standards of performance established and enforced by a self-governing association of colleagues
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforceable ethical codes and performance standards (peer review, ethics committees) are necessary to institutionalize acceptable practice and hold members accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Autonomy and personal responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Autonomy in practice and acceptance of personal responsibility by practitioners
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionals exercise independent judgment and accept responsibility for outcomes and ethical consequences of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of a Profession: Community recognition of unique service
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by the community of providing a unique and essential service
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public and key stakeholders must recognize the occupation as delivering unique, essential services for it to be considered a profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: IABC standard
rubrics_metrics.description: IABC code emphasizes that the principles of professional communication—legal, ethical, and in good taste—apply worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IABC advances competence and ethics via a professional development guide and an ethics review committee; its code sets expectations for global practice (legal, ethical, in good taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: IPRA / Code of Athens
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRA adopted an International Code of Ethics called the 'Code of Athens' based on the UN Declaration of Human Rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPRA promotes professional recognition and high standards internationally and supports professional development in countries where PR is developing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: Global Alliance standards-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Global Alliance sets standards and acts as a clearinghouse for national/international associations; committees include setting standards (ethics, accreditation, curriculum, industry tools, corporate social responsibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GA outcomes include a Global Protocol of Ethics (2003), Position Statement on corporate social responsibility (2004), PR Landscapes reports, and work on core competencies and curriculum; GA facilitates sharing resources among national associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: PRSA functions
rubrics_metrics.description: PRSA fosters exchange of ideas through publications and meetings, promotes professionalism, provides continuing education, and encourages ethical behavior and high standards of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership, chapters, and interest sections provide venues for professional development; PRSA is a major national standard-setting body in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: PRIA membership and accreditation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: PRIA requires a PRIA-accredited tertiary qualification plus a minimum of three years of full-time practice (or five years experience) for full professional membership, and a personal, written commitment to a stringent Code of Ethics; consultancies may apply for Registered Consultancy status with additional Codes of Practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of concrete membership/accreditation standards: educational prerequisites, experience thresholds, written ethical commitment, and consultancy-specific practice codes (client relations, fees, general practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of professional associations: CIPR and CPRS enforcement and development
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPR and CPRS enforce codes of professional and ethical conduct and encourage academic preparation and professional development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CIPR (UK) and CPRS (Canada) run publications, regional/specialist groups, accreditation, and standards enforcement as markers of professionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment and adaptation as basis of contemporary practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustment and adaptation as the basis of contemporary practice (introduced in the sixth edition of the book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary PR practice emphasizes adaptation to changing balance of power in society (research informing management decisions), inclusion of research courses in curricula, and moving beyond the 'journalist-in-residence' model to be part of management decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital age practice expectations: transparency and stakeholder empowerment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet and social media shifted power from media and organizations to individuals, increasing demand for organizational transparency and enabling precisely targeted communication with stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must account for instant, widespread information/misinformation, self-publishing, and the need for targeted stakeholder communication and transparency in organizational messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate social responsibility and professional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional organizations and the Global Alliance promote corporate social responsibility as a dimension of standards and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards-setting bodies produce position statements and encourage CSR as part of ethical and responsible public relations practice.
